title: Comments of Southwest Power Pool Market Monitoring Unit on Southwest Power Pool’s proposal to modify its Open Access Transmission Tariff to add the proposed Conditional High Impact Large Load Service under ER26-1323.
entity: Southwest Power Pool Market Monitoring Unit

documents.name: MMU Comments ER26-1323-000.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                BEFORE THE
                  FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Southwest Power Pool, Inc.                   )                                ER26-1323-000


COMMENTS OF THE SOUTHWEST POWER POOL MARKET MONITORING
                         UNIT

    The Southwest Power Pool Market Monitoring Unit (MMU) respectfully submits these
comments1 on Southwest Power Pool’s (SPP) proposal2 to modify its Open Access
Transmission Tariff (Tariff) to add the proposed Conditional High Impact Large Load
Service (the “CHILLS Proposal”). The objective of the CHILLS Proposal is to establish a
Tariff framework to allow High Impact Large Loads (HILLs) to be served with non-firm
conditional transmission service. The MMU takes no position on the necessity of SPP’s
proposal. If the Commission does find SPP’s proposal is necessary, the MMU finds that
the proposal incorporates Conditional High Impact Large Loads (CHILLs) in a matter that
is fair and efficient, and the Commission should approve the proposal as a just and
reasonable way to effectuate SPP’s goals.

    I.     Background

    The MMU submitted written comments through SPP’s stakeholder process on
December 11, 2025, and December 30, 2025, and diligently participated throughout the
proposal’s development, including presenting and participating in stakeholder meetings
and other feedback processes. Through this process, SPP implemented several
modifications from the MMU’s comments and incorporated them into the filed proposal;
as such, the MMU’s initial concerns that the proposal was unjust and unreasonable were
addressed with the CHILLS Proposal following the recent modifications.



1
  Consistent with FERC Order 719, 18 C.F.R. § 35.28(g)(3)(ii), and SPP OATT Attachment AG,
§1.3, the SPP MMU’s proper role in the SPP stakeholder process is advisory, not decisional. The
SPP MMU has no decision-making role in the ultimate resolution of this matter in any SPP
forum, at the SPP Board, or at FERC. See Wholesale Competition in Regions with Organized
Electric Markets, Order No. 719, 73 Fed. Reg. 64,100 (Oct. 28, 2008), FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶
31,281 (2008); 18 C.F.R. § 35.28(g)(3)(ii) (2024); SPP OATT Attachment AG, § 1.3. SPP MMU
filed a doc-less intervention in this proceeding on February 17, 2026. These comments are timely
as FERC set the deadline for comments as 5pm Eastern Time on March 3, 2026. Combined
Notice of Filings #1, at 3 (Feb. 11, 2026).
2
  Sw. Power Pool, Inc., Revisions to Add the Conditional High Impact Large Load Service (filed
Feb. 10, 2026).
                                                 1
     As part of the dialogue between SPP and the MMU, several items raised by the MMU
were assigned Strategic Initiative Requests (SIRs),3 some were committed to through
working group action items, and some were verbal commitments. For transparency
purposes, the MMU’s comments in this docket focus on those items which were raised, but
not yet incorporated into the CHILLS Proposal, as the MMU believes these items will
benefit from increased clarity, continued tracking, reporting, and future evaluation.
Additionally, we point out a discrepancy, discovered while reviewing the transmittal letter
filed by SPP, with how SPP will calculate “excess hourly generation” for Behind-The-
Meter generation in the proposed Tariff.

    II.     Comments

          A. Overall Comments on the CHILLS Proposal

   First, the MMU believes the interaction between the CHILLS and the to-be-proposed
Demand Response and Peak Demand Assessment4 (RR703) is critical to monitor as the
programs develop. In particular, the MMU supports SPP’s plans to update its Emergency
Operating Plan to specify that Option 15 CHILLs curtailment will be initiated prior to
Reliability Registered Demand Response (RRDR) created under RR703.

    Second, to clarify the processes for CHILLs curtailments and reliability commitments,
the CHILLS Proposal would benefit from a clear statement that SPP will only commit
reliability status resources or make local reliability commitments to supply firm load. In
stakeholder meetings, SPP indicated that it will not make reliability commitments to
support a CHILL, and we recommend that SPP document this in the Tariff and market
protocols.

    Third, under Option 1 CHILLs, SPP would conduct a one-time review to assess whether
a participant has adequate capacity to cover the relevant CHILL. However, we note that it
is possible for a CHILL to become “uncovered” over time. For example, Load Responsible
Entity (LRE) load could grow or existing generation could retire after the one-time review.
The MMU recommends that SPP monitor for CHILLs becoming uncovered over time and,
if necessary, reassess the CHILLS framework considering those findings.

    Fourth, SPP should document what criteria are considered when it determines whether
participants have sufficient capacity to cover a CHILL under Option 1 initially and in the
future. SPP should also reassess allowing LREs to use the same capacity to cover a CHILL
that is used to meet their resource adequacy requirement. Doing so would reduce the

5

                                               2
 potential for risks to resource adequacy while ensuring parties are documenting their
capacity. By using MWs that are already assigned to cover a LRE’s planning reserve
margin to also cover CHILLs, essentially perfect response to CHILL curtailment
instructions are needed so as not to degrade reliability. The MMU recommends SPP
implement oversight mechanisms to ensure CHILLs continue to be evaluated for
sufficiency for long term resource adequacy and do not represent an unmanaged risk.

    Fifth, the MMU recommends that resources designated to cover a CHILL be expressly
barred from also being designated as System Support Resources (also known as RMRs).
This would better align CHILL coverage with the resource’s actual availability and
intended use.

   Sixth, the MMU also recommends additional documentation to improve transparency
and consistency, including (i) how SPP will evaluate and rely on information about run-
time-limited resources and (ii) any standards applicable to run-time-limited resources
dedicated to CHILLs. This would provide transparency to the regulated entities as well as
aim to ensure that resources are available as intended.

   Seventh, the MMU urges that SPP implement strong incentives for CHILLs to respond
to curtailment instructions. SPP should establish clear guidelines for monitoring and
charging market participants for unreserved use of the transmission system. As with the
other recommendations, the process for monitoring and applying such charges should be
documented to provide transparency to regulated entities. Additionally, the MMU
recommends that SPP promptly design and establish a mechanism to address the market
harm associated with uninstructed deviation when CHILLs are not following curtailment.

    Finally, the MMU supports SPP’s efforts to incentivize CHILLs, HILLs, and non-
conforming loads to provide accurate operational load forecasts. Accurate forecasting for
SPP’s Reliability Unit Commitment processes is essential to efficient unit commitment
and proper real-time price formation. If incentives do not exist or are lacking, uncertainty
over the amount of generation needed to serve load will lead to inefficiencies. Delays in
creating incentives for accurate load forecasts will drive inefficient commitments and
distort make-whole payment allocations; this risk increases the more CHILLs and other
large loads come onto the system, so this effort should be expedited.

       B. Specific Comment on Calculation of Excess Generation for Behind-The-
          Meter Generation

    While reviewing the transmittal letter, the MMU discovered an issue with a provision
regarding Behind-The-Meter generation in the proposed Tariff language. In the
transmittal letter, SPP explains that the CHILLS Agreement (CHILLSA) addresses how
Transmission Customers will be charged when CHILLS load, network load, and Behind-
The-Meter generation are located at the same point of delivery. In particular, Section 17.0
of the CHILLSA states that
                                             3
               [T]he Network Load must be adjusted for any excess hourly
              generation above the CHILLS Reserved Capacity. Such excess
              hourly generation will be calculated as the minimum of the
              CHILLS load and the CHILLS Reserved Capacity, plus the
              hourly generation amount, less the CHILLS Reserved
              Capacity. 6
    To see how this calculation would work in practice, consider the following example
of a CHILL, network load, and a Behind-The-Meter generator at the same point of
delivery. Assume the CHILLS load is 100 MW, the CHILLS Reserved Capacity is 120
MW, and hourly generation is 110 MW. The calculation described above would yield an
excess generation of 90 MW:

       Min(100 MW CHILLS load, 120 MW CHILLS Reserved Capacity) +
       110 MW generation – 120 MW CHILLS Reserved Capacity
       = 90 MW excess generation.

    However, it would instead be appropriate for the excess generation to be 10 MW in
this example because the 110 MW of generation exceeds the 100 MW CHILLS load by
10 MW. SPP explains in the transmittal letter that it will then adjust the network load
amount by adding the excess hourly generation MW. This calculation of excess
generation is clearly not correct and would not align with SPP’s intention expressed in
the transmittal letter that these loads and generation be “…properly addressed through
settlement and prevent any netting of loads reported for NITS.” 7




6

                                              4
    III.   Conclusion
   The MMU takes no position on the necessity of SPP’s proposal. If the Commission
does find SPP’s proposal is necessary, the MMU finds that the proposal incorporates
CHILLS in a matter that is fair and efficient, and the Commission should approve the
proposal as a just and reasonable way to effectuate SPP’s goals.


                                        Respectfully submitted,
